patient.name: Declan Murphy
patient.complaint: Yellow eyes, right upper abdominal pain and fever for 10 days
background: Drinks about 1 litre of vodka a day (~40 units) for 15 years
Recent heavy binge after losing his job
Lives alone in Camden; poor diet
No known liver diagnosis; no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a heavy drinker who has jaundice, fever and tender hepatomegaly, and LFTs with an AST:ALT ratio of 2 or more; or a complication question (Wernicke's, encephalopathy, Dupuytren's).

points: 10 days of **yellow eyes** and dark urine.
Dull **right upper quadrant pain**; off his food.
Feverish and exhausted after a two-week binge.

steps.lead: A heavy drinker with sudden liver illness after a binge: **acute alcoholic hepatitis**, an inflammatory injury on top of chronic alcohol use.

visual.title: Where Declan hurts
visual.caption: Tender, enlarged liver in the right upper quadrant extending into the epigastrium.

points: Deeply **jaundiced**; liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, **tender**.
Spider naevi on chest; palmar erythema.
Both ring fingers held bent: thick palmar cords.

steps.lead: Declan has the full set: jaundice, **tender hepatomegaly**, fever, RUQ pain and anorexia with a clear alcohol history, plus early ascites.

steps.title: Declan's LFTs
steps.text: AST is 2.5 times ALT: the alcohol pattern.

visual.title: AST:ALT ratio
visual.label: Declan 2.5
visual.caption: A ratio of 2:1 or more points to alcohol. Viral hepatitis is ALT-dominant with far higher numbers.

steps.lead: Declan's AST of 246 against ALT of 98 gives a ratio of **2.5**: the hallmark of alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.title: Alcoholic hepatitis vs its look-alikes
head: Feature
Alcoholic hepatitis
Viral hepatitis
Cholangitis
rows: Travel, sexual or IV drug risk

steps.q: Overnight Declan becomes confused, unsteady and has nystagmus. What must be given urgently?
steps.r: Confusion, ataxia and eye signs in a drinker is **Wernicke's encephalopathy**: give **IV thiamine** urgently.

steps.lead: Declan's confusion could be **Wernicke's** (thiamine) or **hepatic encephalopathy**: both are emergencies. His palm cords are **Dupuytren's contracture**.

steps.text: Very high transaminases (in the thousands) do **not** fit alcoholic hepatitis. Think viral, ischaemic or paracetamol hepatitis instead.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' with LFTs (AST:ALT ratio), INR as the severity marker, liver ultrasound to exclude obstruction, and Maddrey's discriminant function of 32 or more to decide on steroids.

steps.lead: Declan's diagnosis is clinical plus LFTs: AST:ALT above 2, high bilirubin, mild ALP rise. His **INR** tells you how sick his liver is.

steps.title: Bloods on admission
steps.text: Neutrophilia is common in alcoholic hepatitis, but always look for infection too.

steps.lead: Declan's glucose, FBC, U&Es and **viral screen** exclude other causes, and a **liver ultrasound** looks for obstruction, cirrhosis and ascites.

steps.q: Ultrasound shows a bright, enlarged liver with no dilated ducts. Which score decides if Declan needs steroids?
steps.r: **Maddrey's DF** (from PT and bilirubin) of 32 or more means severe disease: consider prednisolone.

steps.title: Calculating Declan's Maddrey score
nodes: PT 19 s minus control 12 s = 7 s
steps.caption: MDF = 4.6 × (patient PT − control PT) + bilirubin in mg/dL.

visual.title: Maddrey's discriminant function
visual.label: Declan 47
visual.caption: A score of 32 or more predicts high short-term mortality.

steps.lead: Declan's **MDF of 47** is well above 32: severe disease, so steroids are considered.

steps.text: The **INR / prothrombin time** is the best quick marker of acute synthetic failure. Albumin falls slowly, so it reflects chronic disease.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': IV thiamine first in any drinker, alcohol cessation always, and prednisolone only if Maddrey's DF is 32 or more with no infection or GI bleeding.

steps.q: Declan's glucose is 4.2 and he looks malnourished. What goes in first?
steps.r: **IV thiamine** (Pabrinex) first, so glucose does not tip him into Wernicke's.

steps.lead: Declan's plan: **stop alcohol**, IV thiamine, high-protein diet and vitamin supplements. He needs withdrawal cover as he stops.

points: Chest clear; urine and blood cultures negative.
Day 2: no infection or bleeding found.

steps.lead: With **MDF 47** and no infection or GI bleed, Declan starts **prednisolone**.

steps.title: Severe alcoholic hepatitis: steroid decision
nodes: DF ≥ 32 → screen for infection and GI bleed
steps.caption: Infection and GI bleeding are the contraindications to check before steroids.

visual.title: Declan's bilirubin on prednisolone
visual.caption: A falling bilirubin by day 7 shows he is responding to steroids.

steps.text: Do not start **prednisolone** in someone with active infection (SBP, pneumonia) or a **GI bleed**. Treat those first.

steps.lead: Declan's ascites is treated with **diuretics**; any encephalopathy with **lactulose**. If he reaches end-stage, **transplant** needs proven abstinence.
Declan's care follows **NICE NG50** and **BSG** alcohol-related liver disease guidance: assess severity, treat complications, support abstinence.

steps.text: **Alcohol abstinence** is the single intervention that most improves Declan's long-term survival.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why AST exceeds ALT (pyridoxal-5-phosphate deficiency), why glucose without thiamine precipitates Wernicke's, and what Maddrey's DF measures.

steps.lead: Declan's liver breaks alcohol down via **alcohol dehydrogenase** and **CYP2E1**, making **acetaldehyde** and free radicals that injure hepatocytes.
Declan's ALT is low relative to AST because he lacks **pyridoxal-5-phosphate** (B6), and mitochondrial damage releases extra AST.

steps.q: Why is glucose before thiamine dangerous for Declan?
o: Glucose metabolism uses up the remaining thiamine
steps.r: Thiamine is a **cofactor for glucose metabolism**; a glucose load burns the last thiamine and tips him into Wernicke's.

steps.lead: Declan absorbs thiamine poorly and has depleted liver stores, so his brain cannot metabolise glucose: **Wernicke's** risk.
Declan's PT measures **synthetic** function; his bilirubin measures **injury**. Together (MDF) they estimate his short-term mortality.
If Declan keeps drinking, repeated inflammation lays down fibrosis and he will develop **cirrhosis**; episodes like this can decompensate an existing one.

mcq.q: Which LFT pattern is the hallmark of alcoholic hepatitis?
Which vitamin deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
Which hand sign is associated with alcohol excess?
mcq.r: **Dupuytren's**: fixed flexion of the 4th/5th fingers, often bilateral.

mcq.q: Alcohol history + jaundice + confusion suggests what?
mcq.r: A **medical emergency**: alcoholic hepatitis with encephalopathy.

mcq.q: Which value is the main marker of severity in alcoholic hepatitis?
What Maddrey's discriminant function indicates severe disease?
Which two values are used to calculate Maddrey's DF?
Which drug is given first-line to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy?
Which contraindication must be excluded before prednisolone?
Why is ALT lower than AST in alcoholic hepatitis?
o: ALT is cleared by the kidney
mcq.r: **Pyridoxal-5-phosphate (B6)** is needed more for ALT synthesis.

prompts.q: What is alcoholic hepatitis and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a heavy drinker with fever, jaundice and a tender liver.

points.p: Acute inflammation of the liver from excessive alcohol, on a chronic background

points.why: Tender liver separates it from simple fatty liver.
Fever can occur without infection, but always look for one.

points.p: May precipitate decompensation of cirrhosis (ascites, encephalopathy)
points.why: Signs of chronic liver disease may also be present.

prompts.q: Which blood pattern points to alcoholic hepatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: compare AST with ALT, and look at GGT and MCV.

points.why: ALP only mildly raised, unlike obstruction.

prompts.q: Which complications and associated signs must you recognise in alcoholic hepatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a confused drinker needs thiamine before anything else.

points.why: Fixed flexion, uncorrectable passively, often bilateral.

prompts.q: How do you tell alcoholic hepatitis from viral hepatitis and cholangitis on LFTs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the size and pattern of the enzymes decides it.

points.p: Viral hepatitis: ALT in the thousands, ALT greater than AST
Cholangitis/obstruction: ALP and GGT dominant with dilated ducts
points.why: Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain.

points.p: Alcoholic hepatitis: modest transaminases, AST ≥2× ALT, high GGT

prompts.q: Which investigations confirm alcoholic hepatitis and exclude other causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical picture plus LFTs, then rule out the rest.

points.p: LFTs: AST and ALT raised with AST:ALT >2, bilirubin up, ALP mildly up
points.why: Diagnosis is clinical plus LFT pattern plus history.
Neutrophilia is common; screen for infection.
Excludes biliary obstruction, shows cirrhosis or ascites.

prompts.q: How is severity assessed and what cut-off changes management?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one score, one number.

points.why: The standard severity score in the notes.

points.p: Calculated from prothrombin time and bilirubin

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of alcoholic hepatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what everyone gets, before any steroid decision.

points.why: Improves long-term survival more than anything else.

points.p: Supportive: high-protein diet and vitamin supplements

prompts.q: When do you give steroids, when not, and how are complications managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: score first, contraindications second.

points.p: Contraindicated by active infection or GI bleeding
Diuretics for ascites, lactulose for encephalopathy
Liver transplant is definitive for end-stage disease

prompts.q: How does alcohol injure the liver, and why is the AST:ALT ratio raised?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the metabolite and the vitamin.

points.p: Alcohol dehydrogenase and CYP2E1 generate acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species
points.why: Cause lipid peroxidation and hepatocyte injury.

points.p: Pyridoxal-5-phosphate (B6) deficiency reduces ALT synthesis more than AST
points.why: The main reason ALT stays low.

points.p: Ongoing inflammation and fibrogenesis lead to cirrhosis

prompts.q: Why does alcohol excess cause Wernicke's, and what does Maddrey's DF measure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: thiamine is a cofactor; PT and bilirubin are two different functions.

points.p: Alcohol impairs thiamine absorption and depletes liver stores
Thiamine is a cofactor for cerebral glucose metabolism; glucose without thiamine precipitates Wernicke's
MDF: prothrombin time (synthesis) + bilirubin (injury) estimates short-term mortality

glossary.Alcoholic hepatitis: Acute inflammation of the liver caused by heavy alcohol use, often after a binge.
glossary.Hepatomegaly: Enlarged liver, felt below the right costal margin.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellow skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.
glossary.RUQ: Right upper quadrant of the abdomen, where the liver and gallbladder lie.
glossary.AST: Aspartate aminotransferase: liver (and muscle) enzyme, typically at least twice ALT in alcoholic hepatitis.
glossary.ALT: Alanine aminotransferase: a liver-specific enzyme; very high levels suggest viral or toxic hepatitis.
glossary.AST:ALT ratio: AST divided by ALT; a value of 2 or more is the hallmark of alcohol-related liver injury.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase: enzyme raised mainly in biliary obstruction and bone disease.
glossary.GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase: liver enzyme induced by alcohol, raised in heavy drinkers.
glossary.Bilirubin: Yellow breakdown product of haemoglobin, cleared by the liver; high levels cause jaundice.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio: measures clotting time; raised when the liver cannot make clotting factors.
glossary.Prothrombin time: Time for blood to clot via the extrinsic pathway; prolonged in liver synthetic failure.
glossary.PT: Prothrombin time: clotting test used, with bilirubin, in Maddrey's discriminant function.
glossary.Hypoalbuminaemia: Low blood albumin, from poor liver synthesis or malnutrition.
glossary.Maddrey's Discriminant Function: Severity score from prothrombin time and bilirubin; 32 or more means severe alcoholic hepatitis.
glossary.MDF: Maddrey's discriminant function, the severity score that guides steroid use.
glossary.Wernicke's encephalopathy: Acute brain dysfunction from thiamine deficiency: confusion, ataxia and eye movement problems.
glossary.Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Wernicke's encephalopathy progressing to Korsakoff's permanent memory loss with confabulation.
glossary.Thiamine: Vitamin B1, a cofactor for glucose metabolism; deficiency causes Wernicke's encephalopathy.
glossary.Pabrinex: Brand of intravenous high-dose B vitamins including thiamine, used in alcohol-dependent patients.
glossary.Dupuytren's contracture: Thickening of the palmar fascia causing fixed flexion of the ring and little fingers.
glossary.Hepatic encephalopathy: Confusion and drowsiness from toxins such as ammonia that a failing liver cannot clear.
glossary.Asterixis: Flapping tremor of outstretched hands, seen in hepatic encephalopathy.
glossary.Spider naevi: Small red spots with radiating vessels on the upper body, a sign of chronic liver disease.
glossary.Palmar erythema: Reddening of the palms, a sign of chronic liver disease.
glossary.Ascites: Fluid in the peritoneal cavity, often from portal hypertension.
glossary.Cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with nodules, causing portal hypertension and liver failure.
glossary.Decompensation: When chronic liver disease tips into failure: ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding.
glossary.Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid used in severe alcoholic hepatitis when Maddrey's DF is 32 or more.
glossary.Lactulose: Osmotic laxative that reduces ammonia absorption, used for hepatic encephalopathy.
glossary.Neutrophilia: Raised neutrophil count, common in alcoholic hepatitis even without infection.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume; a raised MCV (macrocytosis) is common with heavy alcohol use.
glossary.Acetaldehyde: Toxic first breakdown product of alcohol that damages liver cells.
glossary.Alcohol dehydrogenase: Liver enzyme that converts ethanol to acetaldehyde.
glossary.CYP2E1: Cytochrome P450 enzyme induced by chronic drinking; metabolises alcohol and makes free radicals.
glossary.Reactive oxygen species: Unstable oxygen molecules that damage cell membranes, proteins and DNA.
glossary.Lipid peroxidation: Free-radical damage to fats in cell membranes, injuring hepatocytes.
glossary.Pyridoxal-5-phosphate: Active vitamin B6; needed more for ALT than AST synthesis, so its deficiency lowers ALT.
glossary.Fibrogenesis: The laying down of scar tissue (collagen) in an injured organ.
glossary.Chlordiazepoxide: Long-acting benzodiazepine used to cover alcohol withdrawal.
glossary.NICE NG50: NICE guideline on assessing and managing cirrhosis in people over 16.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man has a 1 week history of yellow skin, fever and right upper quadrant pain. He drinks 30 units of alcohol a day. His liver is enlarged and tender. His temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 104 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of jaundice in a drinker: decide the liver pattern.

clues: yellow skin, fever and right upper quadrant pain
steps.x: Jaundice, fever, **tender hepatomegaly** in a heavy drinker; labs show AST 2.5× ALT and high GGT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alcoholic hepatitis**.

elim: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back and a high amylase.
Fatty liver is usually asymptomatic: no fever, jaundice or tenderness.
Cholangitis has an obstructive picture with ALP dominant.
Hepatitis A gives ALT in the thousands, ALT greater than AST.

steps.x: **C. Alcoholic hepatitis.** Rule: drinker + fever + tender liver + AST:ALT ≥2.

technique.stem: A 44 year old woman with alcoholic hepatitis is admitted with jaundice. The team wants a single blood test that best reflects how severely her liver's synthetic function is impaired right now.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Asks for a marker of **synthetic** function, acutely.
Synthesis means clotting factors or albumin; 'right now' favours the fast-changing one.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prothrombin time / INR**, also used in Maddrey's DF.

elim: ALP reflects biliary obstruction.
ALT reflects hepatocyte damage, not synthesis.
Amylase is for pancreatitis.
GGT reflects alcohol use and cholestasis.

steps.x: **E. Prothrombin time.** Rule: enzymes show damage; PT/INR shows function.

technique.stem: A 49 year old man has alcoholic hepatitis. He has received intravenous thiamine and stopped drinking. His Maddrey's discriminant function is 48. Chest X-ray, urine culture and blood cultures are clear, ascitic neutrophils are 40 cells/mm³, and there is no gastrointestinal bleeding.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step after supportive care: is a steroid indicated?
MDF ≥32 = severe; infection and bleeding excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prednisolone**.

elim: Terlipressin is for variceal bleeding.
Transplant is for end-stage disease after a period of abstinence.
NAC is for paracetamol overdose.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is for PBC, not alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: **D. Oral prednisolone.** Rule: MDF ≥32, no infection, no bleed = steroid.

technique.stem: A 40 year old man who drinks heavily is found confused and malnourished. A doctor gives intravenous 5% glucose for a capillary glucose of 3.6 mmol/L. An hour later he is ataxic and has ophthalmoplegia.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
o: Glucose metabolism uses up remaining thiamine

steps.x: A mechanism: why did glucose make him worse?
Thiamine-depleted drinker given glucose, then **Wernicke's** signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism; the glucose load used it up.

elim: Glucose does not raise ammonia.
Osmotic demyelination follows rapid sodium correction.
Hypokalaemia causes weakness and arrhythmia, not ophthalmoplegia.
This is not lactic acidosis; it is thiamine depletion.

steps.x: **A. Glucose uses up remaining thiamine.** Rule: thiamine before glucose in drinkers.

practice.stem: A 46 year old man has a 2 week history of jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and poor appetite. He has drunk two bottles of wine a day for 10 years and recently increased this. His liver is enlarged and tender. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 114/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Jaundice, fever and tender hepatomegaly in a heavy drinker with AST:ALT above 2 is alcoholic hepatitis. Cholangitis would show an obstructive pattern with a high ALP.

steps.x: Diagnosis: fever and jaundice in a drinker.

clues: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and poor appetite
two bottles of wine a day
steps.x: Heavy drinking with a recent increase; tender hepatomegaly; labs: AST:ALT ~2.5, normal amylase.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alcoholic hepatitis**.

elim: Cholangitis has an ALP-dominant obstructive picture and dilated ducts.
Cholecystitis has Murphy's sign and rarely deep jaundice.
Amylase is normal.
HCC is a mass with weight loss, not an acute febrile illness.

steps.x: **D. Alcoholic hepatitis.** Rule: AST:ALT ≥2 + tender liver + alcohol.

practice.stem: A 51 year old woman is admitted with jaundice and a tender enlarged liver. She has drunk heavily for many years and stopped 3 days ago. Her mean cell volume is 104 fL and GGT is 640 IU/L. She has no history of travel, intravenous drug use or new medicines.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on her liver function tests?
o: ALP rise greater than transaminase rise
practice.e: Alcoholic hepatitis gives modest transaminases with AST at least twice ALT. ALT in the thousands suggests viral, ischaemic or paracetamol hepatitis.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: predict the LFT pattern.
Macrocytosis and a high GGT confirm alcohol; tender liver means hepatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **AST:ALT ≥2**.

elim: An ALP-dominant pattern is cholestatic/obstructive.
ALT in the thousands is viral or toxic hepatitis.
Isolated unconjugated bilirubin is Gilbert's or haemolysis.
A tender, inflamed liver will raise transaminases.

steps.x: **C. AST:ALT 2:1 or greater.** The hallmark of alcoholic hepatitis.

practice.stem: A 43 year old man with alcoholic hepatitis became confused on the ward 2 days after admission. He is unsteady on his feet and has horizontal nystagmus with bilateral lateral rectus weakness. He was given intravenous glucose overnight for a low capillary glucose. He has no flapping tremor. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his confusion?
practice.e: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia after glucose without thiamine is Wernicke's encephalopathy. Hepatic encephalopathy causes a flapping tremor, not eye signs.

steps.x: Cause of confusion in a drinker with hepatitis.
Classic triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, after glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wernicke's encephalopathy** (thiamine deficiency).

elim: Withdrawal causes tremor, sweating, tachycardia and hallucinations, not ophthalmoplegia.
Hepatic encephalopathy causes asterixis, which is absent.
He has been given glucose.
Subdural would give headache and focal signs, not this triad.

steps.x: **E. Wernicke's encephalopathy.** Rule: thiamine before glucose.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with alcoholic hepatitis has had difficulty gripping for a year. Both ring and little fingers are held flexed at the metacarpophalangeal joints and cannot be straightened passively. A thick cord is palpable in each palm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding?
practice.e: Fixed flexion of the 4th/5th fingers with a palpable palmar cord, often bilateral, is Dupuytren's contracture, associated with alcohol excess. Swan neck is rheumatoid.

steps.x: Name the hand sign.
Fixed, passively uncorrectable flexion of the 4th/5th fingers with a palmar cord.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dupuytren's contracture**.

elim: Clubbing affects nail beds, not flexion.
Heberden's nodes are DIP osteophytes in osteoarthritis.
Koilonychia is spoon nails in iron deficiency.
Swan neck is a rheumatoid deformity.

steps.x: **B. Dupuytren's contracture.**

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis has been stable for a year. After a 3 week binge he has deepening jaundice, a tender enlarged liver, fever and increasing abdominal swelling. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. There is no haematemesis or melaena.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his decompensation?
practice.e: A binge with fever, tender hepatomegaly and AST:ALT above 2 has caused acute alcoholic hepatitis, precipitating decompensation. Ascitic neutrophils below 250 exclude SBP.

steps.x: Cause of decompensation in cirrhosis.
Recent binge, tender liver, AST:ALT ~2.7; ascitic neutrophils normal, AFP normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alcoholic hepatitis** on cirrhosis.

elim: AFP is normal and there is no mass or weight loss.
PVT would not explain the binge, fever and AST pattern.
Ascitic neutrophils are below 250 cells/mm³.
No haematemesis or melaena.

steps.x: **A. Alcoholic hepatitis.** It commonly decompensates existing cirrhosis.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman has 10 days of jaundice, nausea and right upper quadrant discomfort. She drinks about 8 units of alcohol a day. Her liver is tender and 3 cm enlarged. Her temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. Hepatitis serology and autoantibodies are negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Jaundice and a tender liver with AST:ALT above 2, very high GGT and macrocytosis in a daily drinker is alcoholic hepatitis. Negative serology and autoantibodies exclude viral and autoimmune causes.

steps.x: Diagnosis of hepatitic jaundice.

clues: Hepatitis serology and autoantibodies are negative
steps.x: Daily drinking, tender liver; labs: AST:ALT 2.6, GGT very high, macrocytosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alcoholic hepatitis**.

elim: Serology is negative and ALT would be far higher.
Autoantibodies are negative.
NAFLD is ALT-dominant and not febrile and jaundiced.
PBC is cholestatic (ALP), AMA positive, in older women.

steps.x: **B. Alcoholic hepatitis.**

practice.stem: A 50 year old man is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. His team needs to decide whether he should receive corticosteroids. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate assessment to guide this decision?
practice.e: Maddrey's discriminant function (prothrombin time and bilirubin) of 32 or more indicates severe alcoholic hepatitis and prompts steroids. Here it is about 54. Child-Pugh grades cirrhosis.

steps.x: Which score guides steroids in alcoholic hepatitis?
Steroid decision = severity score from PT and bilirubin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Maddrey's DF**: 4.6 × 8 + 17 = ~54, severe.

elim: Child-Pugh grades cirrhosis severity.
Glasgow-Blatchford is for upper GI bleeding.
Ranson is for pancreatitis.
Ammonia does not guide steroid therapy.

steps.x: **C. Maddrey's DF.** Rule: ≥32 = consider prednisolone.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man who drinks heavily has jaundice, fever and a tender enlarged liver. His AST is 190 IU/L, ALT 80 IU/L and ALP 170 IU/L. The team wants to exclude biliary obstruction and look for cirrhosis and ascites.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging?
practice.e: Liver ultrasound is the first-line imaging in alcoholic hepatitis: it excludes duct dilatation and shows cirrhosis and ascites. MRCP and ERCP are for confirmed obstruction.

steps.x: Initial imaging, not definitive.
Fast, safe, bedside answer to all three.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Liver ultrasound**.

elim: CT is not first-line and uses contrast and radiation.
ERCP is invasive and therapeutic, for proven stones.
Biopsy is not routine and is risky with a raised INR.
MRCP follows an ultrasound showing dilated ducts.

steps.x: **E. Liver ultrasound.**

practice.stem: A 48 year old man who drinks heavily is brought to the Emergency Department confused and jaundiced. He is thin and unkempt. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg and capillary glucose 3.9 mmol/L. He has a tender enlarged liver.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: IV thiamine comes first in any confused, malnourished drinker, before glucose, to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy. Prednisolone waits for a Maddrey score and infection screen.

steps.x: Initial management: the first drug.
Malnourished drinker, confused, borderline glucose: thiamine-depleted.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV thiamine** first.

elim: Glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's.
Lactulose treats encephalopathy, but thiamine comes first.
Steroids need a Maddrey score and no infection.
Rifaximin is add-on encephalopathy prophylaxis.

steps.x: **B. Intravenous thiamine.**

practice.stem: A 53 year old man has severe alcoholic hepatitis with a Maddrey's discriminant function of 44. He has a productive cough. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Chest X-ray shows right lower zone consolidation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: MDF 44 would normally prompt prednisolone, but active infection (pneumonia) is a contraindication. Treat the infection and withhold steroids.

steps.x: Severe disease, but check contraindications.
Severe hepatitis plus **active infection**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat pneumonia; **no steroids** while infected.

elim: Terlipressin is for variceal bleeding or hepatorenal syndrome.
Transplant is not for acute alcoholic hepatitis with active drinking.
Steroids are contraindicated by active infection.
Rifaximin is for encephalopathy.

steps.x: **A. IV antibiotics, withhold prednisolone.** Rule: infection or GI bleed = no steroids.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man is recovering from alcoholic hepatitis. His bilirubin is falling after a course of prednisolone. He asks what will make the biggest difference to whether he survives the next few years.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Alcohol cessation is essential and is the main determinant of long-term survival. Transplant is reserved for end-stage disease after proven abstinence.

steps.x: Long-term management that most improves survival.
Acute episode settled; the cause must be removed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Abstinence from alcohol**.

elim: Cholestyramine treats pruritus only.
Transplant needs abstinence and end-stage disease.
Steroids are a short course, not long-term.
Propranolol prevents variceal bleeding in cirrhosis.

steps.x: **B. Complete abstinence.**

practice.stem: A 50 year old man who drinks heavily has jaundice and tender hepatomegaly. His AST is 240 IU/L and ALT 90 IU/L. A student asks why the ALT is so much lower than the AST.
